Unusual palette that was clearly chosen: oxblood red ground with teal-grey foliage, saffron, blush pink and powder blue, applied consistently across every frame.

Real texture work: a woven, fabric-like grain on the ground, risograph-style stipple and halftone shading on the objects, and grainy cast shadows that lift objects off the surface like paper cut-outs.
The background pattern changes and reflows between frames (eyes appear, flowers shift), which implies the wallpaper is choreographed and alive rather than a static plate.
Drawing is asymmetric and characterful (tiger expression, glove cuffs, cannon wheel). It isn't clip art.

The motion implied between frames looks like object swaps. Transformations would show more invention: the tiger's stripes becoming foliage, the cannon firing into the next object.

tells: Mature, consistent house style for an explainer: flat vector with rim lights, glowing edges, saturated gradient skies and a character cast with clear personality (villain at the STOP button, the birds' memory game, the mammoth).
Every frame is a different scene with a different metaphor (control room, card game, heat-map title, mammoth), so the narrative choreography is clear rather than one repeated layout.
The title card integrates bold rounded type with a stylised temperature map, so the type sits inside the image rather than on top of a slide.
Weakness: this is a well-known, widely imitated explainer idiom. The subtitle captions are default small white sans, and the light is graphic rather than material.
gaps: The style is the genre standard. It needs a visual idea specific to this topic (an Ice Age told through texture, frost or material) rather than the generic house look.
The burned-in captions are default and compete with the image. Design a caption system that suits the piece, or integrate the words into the scenes.
Flat gradient lighting with no texture or material. Adding grain, frost or a tactile layer would match A's depth.

tells: Hand-painted dry-brush strokes with real bristle texture and opacity variation, a gestural quality rather than vector defaults.

The changes between frames suggest stroke-on painting choreography, with varied structures (diagonal lattice, grid, plaid).
Against it: the primary-colour Mondrian reference is familiar territory, and the frames feel more like sketchbook than finished. The image is uneven and there is no type.
gaps: The Mondrian/NYC reference is well-worn. It needs a twist or a narrative beat that only this piece could have.
Compositions are loose and in places arbitrary (the green/blue plaid frame). Each frame should hold up as a poster, with tighter balance and focal hierarchy.
No typography and no layering of depth. A's material richness and the density it achieves within one controlled palette are missing.

Frames move from a figurative spire through a grid and diagonals to a city-street grid with yellow taxis. That progression implies a stroke-on and transformation choreography with a clear idea behind it.
The aspect ratio changes between frames and some compositions look unfinished or loose, which reads as sketchbook energy more than final polish.

The palette is unusual and controlled: deep oxblood red with teal leaves, sun-yellow, and cream.
Rich textures (fabric weave, risograph-style grain, stipple shading) make the objects feel printed and tactile.

A clear motif system (tiger, tarot cards with a horseshoe, cannon, strongman's barbell) on a living folk-art pattern with watching eyes. Every frame works as a poster, and the border elements shift from frame to frame, implying animated choreography.
gaps: Vary scale and camera more; each frame is one centred hero object, so the rhythm risks feeling repetitive.
Add interaction between objects and the pattern so the motion shows weight and narrative, not just hero objects swapping in.
Introduce one surprising twist or typographic moment that pays off the fortune-teller and circus theme.

defects: There is little motion inside each shot. Each 1/6 s pair barely changes apart from a slow camera drift or a word fading in, so the motion is mostly dissolves and slow camera moves over a still set.
The type reveals are plain opacity or wipe-ins ('wa' simply appears between frames). Nothing in the grain or the light drives the reveal, and nothing settles or overshoots.

Continuity between shots is broken. The window and tree reflection in the coffee appears only in the later shots, and the bowl changes colour from cream to grey-blue, so it reads as separately rendered setups rather than one space.

Several frames are cropped awkwardly. 'peach' is cut on the left edge and runs under the bowl, 'ashe' is cut off by the frame, 'Ethiopia' is clipped by the spoon, and the bowl is cut at the top of the close-up.
The shallow depth of field makes the type soft and smeared in the 'washed' and 'Ethiopia' shots. The focus pulls look like a fixed lens setting, not a choice made for the shot.
The soundtrack cuts off hard at about 19.5 kHz, as if low-pass filtered. The hit pattern is a near-regular grid that does not clearly line up with the 2.5 s cut rhythm.
The pace fails the benchmark. The longest shot is 5 s and the median is 2.5 s, and the opening and the hold before the pack shot are dead air.
gaps: Choreography. The idea of tasting notes coming up out of the wood grain is strong, but it never becomes motion. The grain should flow, burn or swell into each letterform, with the camera and the reveal handing off to each other, instead of a fade over a slow push-in.

Arc and pacing. Every shot follows the same pattern (a note fades in, then a slow camera drift), so energy stays flat until the pull-back. A top studio would cut faster (about 1.5 s or less), make the notes escalate, and build to a real peak around 10 s before the Guji resolve.

Sound to picture. The audio is a busy, evenly hitting bed with a drop at about 9.8 s and a swell at 10.3 s. It is not built to land on the type reveals or the cuts, and there is no material sound design such as wood, ceramic or liquid. The drop is the one moment that could work if it were cut to the reveal.
